{{redirect|Come to Mama|the Lady Gaga song|Come to Mama (Lady Gaga song)}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2021}} {{Use British English|date=June 2012}} {{Infobox album | name = White City: A Novel | type = [[Studio album]] | artist = [[Pete Townshend]] | cover = White City A Novel.jpg | border = yes | alt = | released = {{start date|1985|11|11|df=y}} | recorded = November 1984 – July 1985 | venue = | studio = *[[Eel Pie Studios]], [[Twickenham]] *Eel Pie Studios, [[Soho]] *[[AIR Oxford Circus|AIR]], London | genre = {{hlist|[[Rock music|Rock]]|[[pop rock]]}} | length = {{duration|m=38|s=27}} | label = [[Atco Records|Atco]] (US) | producer = [[Chris Thomas (record producer)|Chris Thomas]] | prev_title = [[Scoop (album)|Scoop]] | prev_year = 1983 | next_title = [[Deep End Live!]] | next_year = 1986 | misc = {{Singles | name = White City: A Novel | type = [[Studio album]] | single1 = [[Face the Face]] | single1date = 1985 | single2 = [[Give Blood (song)|Give Blood]] | single2date = 1985 | single3 = Secondhand Love | single3date = 1986 }} }} {{Music ratings | rev1 = [[AllMusic]] | rev1Score = {{Rating|3.5|5}}{{AllMusic|class=album|id=r20356}} | rev2 = ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' | rev2Score = (positive){{cite web |url=http://www.rollingstone.com/artists/petetownshend/albums/album/302857/review/6067802/white_city_a_novel |title=Pete Townshend: White City (A Novel) : Music Reviews : Rolling Stone |website=www.rollingstone.com |access-date=13 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080415171931/http://www.rollingstone.com/artists/petetownshend/albums/album/302857/review/6067802/white_city_a_novel |archive-date=15 April 2008 |url-status=dead}} }} '''''White City: A Novel''''' is the fifth solo [[Album#Studio|studio album]] by the English [[rock musician]] [[Pete Townshend]], released on 11 November 1985 by [[Atco Records]]. The album was produced by [[Chris Thomas (record producer)|Chris Thomas]] (who had also produced Townshend's previous two albums, ''[[Empty Glass]]'' and ''[[All the Best Cowboys Have Chinese Eyes]]'') and it was recorded by [[Bill Price (record producer)|Bill Price]] at three separate [[recording studio]]s in [[London]], England: both of the [[Eel Pie Studios|Eel Pie studios]], and [[AIR Oxford Circus|AIR]]. The album peaked at No. 70 on the [[UK Albums Chart]], and at No. 26 on the US [[Billboard 200|''Billboard'' 200]]. The album also reached the Top 20 in five other countries, Australia, Germany, New Zealand, Sweden and Switzerland. == Concept == A loose [[concept album]], its title refers to a story (called a "novel" in the album title) that accompanies the album, which takes place in a low-income [[housing estate]] in the [[West End of London|West London]] district of [[White City, London|White City]], near where Townshend had grown up. The story tells of cultural conflict, racial tension and youthful hopes and dreams in the 1960s – a world of "[[Child prostitution|prostituted children]]", "roads leading to darkness, leading home" and despairing residents living in "cells" with views of "dustbins and a [[Ford Cortina]]". The song "White City Fighting", which features [[Pink Floyd]]'s [[David Gilmour]] on guitar, tells listeners that the White City was "a black, violent place" where "battles were won, and battles were blown, at the height of the White City fighting". Biographer Mark Wilkerson quotes Townshend’s explanation for the “a novel” subtitle: “‘Well, I thought, if I could get away with Rock Opera . . .’ Pete told Dan Neer, ‘[that’s] a bit of a gag, you know, to address the fact that I’d been working as a book publisher lately and that if I was gonna make a record and a video, that I should call it a novel.’”''Who Are You: The Life of Pete Townshend'' (London: Omnibus Press, 2008), 378. The album opens with crashing guitar chords (also played by Gilmour {{cite web | title= Coolwalkingsmoothtalking Liner Notes | work= The Hypertext Who – Bill's Pete Townshend Pages | date= 2008-08-01 | url= http://www.thewho.net/petetownshend/bestofln.htm | access-date= 2014-04-16 | url-status= dead | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131214013633/http://www.thewho.net/petetownshend/bestofln.htm | archive-date= 2013-12-14 }} ) that capture a feeling of urban chaos, leading into "[[Give Blood (song)|Give Blood]]", a song with Townshend's moral lyrics demanding listeners to "give blood, but you may find that blood is not enough". {{cite web | title= Give Blood Lyrics | url= https://genius.com/Pete-townshend-give-blood-lyrics | access-date= 2018-05-17 }} ==Film== The disc also mentions a film based on the album, directed and "adapted for longform video" by [[Richard Lowenstein]]. The 60-minute video, entitled ''White City: The Music Movie'', was released by [[Vestron Pictures|Vestron Music Video]] in 1985 and stars [[Pete Townshend]], [[Andrew Wilde (actor)|Andrew Wilde]] and [[Frances Barber]]. The [[videotape]] also features exclusive footage of Townshend discussing the album and film, and the premiere performance of "Night School". That song, in a different form, would be included on [[Hip-O]]'s 2006 reissue as a bonus track. ==Album contents== The track "White City Fighting" originated as a composition written by [[David Gilmour]] for his 1984 solo album ''[[About Face (album)|About Face]]''.{{Cite book | edition = [Updated ed.] | publisher = Omnibus | isbn = 0-7119-4109-2 | last = Miles | first = Barry |author2=Andy Mabbett | title = Pink Floyd the visual documentary | location = London | year = 1994 }} He asked Townshend to supply lyrics, but felt that he could not relate to them, so Townshend used the song instead with Gilmour playing guitar. Gilmour sent the same tune to [[Roy Harper (singer)|Roy Harper]], whose lyrics had the same effect as Townshend's on Gilmour. Harper used the result, "Hope", which has a markedly slower tempo, on his 1985 album ''[[Whatever Happened to Jugula?]]'' with [[Nick Harper|Harper's son Nick]] on guitar. ==Reception== ''[[Cash Box]]'' said that "Secondhand Love" "continues Townshend’s penchant for brilliant songwriting and tough, hard-hitting performance."{{cite magazine|title=Single Releases|magazine=Cash Box|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/80s/1986/CB-1986-03-22.pdf|date=March 22, 1986|accessdate=2022-08-03|page=9}} ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' said it's "delivered with [Townshend's] customary intensity."{{cite magazine|magazine=Billboard|date=March 22, 1986|accessdate=2022-08-03|page=79|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XyQEAAAAMBAJ|title=Reviews}} ''[[Spin (magazine)|Spin]]'' said, "There's really only one thing | can be sure about: ''White City'' is one of the most pretentiously boring records I've heard in quite some time. You begin to wonder why Townshend's still making records if he can't even find the inspiration to sound like himself."{{cite magazine| magazine= [[Spin (magazine)|Spin]] | title=Spins|author=Billy
